questions.stem: For a colliding passenger, the force felt is smaller when:

options.text: The collision is over in a shorter instant
options.explanation: A shorter contact time would raise the force, not lower it.

options.text: The passenger carries more momentum into the crash
options.explanation: More momentum means a bigger change to unload, which raises the force.

options.text: The collision time is stretched out
options.explanation: Force is the rate of momentum change, so spreading it over more time lowers the force.

options.text: The vehicle is made heavier
options.explanation: Extra mass enlarges the momentum; it does nothing to soften the impact.

questions.stem: A seat belt protects its wearer mainly by:

options.text: Holding the passenger perfectly rigid so no stretch occurs
options.explanation: A rigid hold would remove the stretch that lengthens the stopping time.

options.text: Stretching a little, so the wearer's momentum takes longer to fall to zero
options.explanation: The slight stretch extends the contact time and cuts the peak force.

options.text: Increasing the wearer's forward momentum
options.explanation: The belt changes how quickly momentum is lost, not how much there is.

options.text: Keeping the passenger loose so the interior absorbs the hit
options.explanation: Loose passengers strike the interior; the belt's job is to hold them and stretch gently.

questions.stem: Crumple zones protect the people inside a car by:

options.text: Making the car bounce back off the obstacle
options.explanation: The zones deform; they do not make the car rebound.

options.text: Keeping the bodywork undamaged in a crash
options.explanation: The zones are meant to deform — some damage is designed in.

options.text: Cutting the car's speed before contact happens
options.explanation: They act during the collision itself, not on the approach.

options.text: Crushing in a planned way, which extends how long the car takes to stop
options.explanation: The controlled crush lengthens the stop and lowers the force on the passengers.

questions.stem: Vehicle safety features absorb impact energy chiefly by:

options.text: Changing shape
options.explanation: Deforming structures soak up the crash energy as they give way.

options.text: Adding mass to the vehicle
options.explanation: Extra mass would enlarge the momentum instead of absorbing energy.

options.text: Reducing the car's speed before the impact
options.explanation: These features work inside the collision, not before it.

options.text: Heating up the passenger compartment
options.explanation: Heat plays no designed role in the protection.

questions.stem: A truck striking a wall at speed needs a very long contact time because:

options.text: Trucks are built with softer crumple zones than cars
options.explanation: Material softness is not the reason; the size of the momentum is.

options.text: Its large mass and high speed together give it enormous momentum
options.explanation: A huge momentum change must be spread over a long time to keep the force down.

options.text: Its momentum stays small even at high speed
options.explanation: A massive, fast truck carries an enormous momentum.

options.text: The wall decides how hard to push back
options.explanation: The impact force follows from the truck's momentum change and the contact time alone.

questions.stem: State what is meant by contact time.
questions.modelAnswer: It is the duration for which the person stays in touch with whatever they have struck — a soft, giving contact makes it longer.

questions.stem: Name the three main safety features built into a vehicle.
questions.modelAnswer: Seat belts, airbags and crumple zones — all absorb crash energy by deforming and all stretch the time over which the force acts.

questions.stem: Explain why crumple zones leave a car looking more damaged than expected, even after a small collision.
questions.modelAnswer: Crumple zones at the front and rear are built to deform on purpose; the deliberate crumpling extends the vehicle's stopping time, so the passengers feel a smaller force — the visible damage is the price of that gentler stop.

questions.stem: A designer must choose between a rigid metal dashboard and a padded, deformable one. Use the idea of momentum to argue for the padded design.
questions.modelAnswer: The padded surface lengthens the contact time when a passenger is thrown forward, so the same momentum change spreads over a longer interval; with force as the rate of change of momentum, the padded dash delivers a smaller force and a lower injury risk.

questions.stem: A crash mat protects a falling gymnast chiefly by:

options.text: Reducing the gymnast's momentum to nothing instantly
options.explanation: An instant stop would mean a huge force — the opposite of protection.

options.text: Making the gymnast lighter in mid-air
options.explanation: The mat acts on landing; it cannot change the gymnast's mass.

options.text: Lowering the gymnast's speed before touchdown
options.explanation: The mat waits below; it works during contact, not during the descent.

options.text: Extending the time the gymnast spends in contact with the mat
options.explanation: A longer contact time slows the rate of momentum change, so the force drops.

questions.stem: Why can a child manage with a thinner mat than an adult?

options.text: A smaller mass brings less momentum, so less cushioning time is needed
options.explanation: With less momentum to unload, a thinner mat still keeps the force low.

options.text: Children's bones are more flexible than adults'
options.explanation: The reasoning is about momentum, not biology.

options.text: Thin mats work only for light users
options.explanation: Mats work for everyone; thickness must match the momentum involved.

options.text: Children always fall from lower heights
options.explanation: Height is a separate factor; the thinner mat here follows from mass.

questions.stem: A playground's cushioned surface protects falling children by:

options.text: Stopping children from ever reaching the ground
options.explanation: Children still land; the surface changes how the landing unfolds.

options.text: Lengthening their contact time with the ground
options.explanation: More contact time spreads the momentum change and shrinks the force.

options.text: Reducing the children's weight
options.explanation: Weight is unchanged; the surface changes the timing of the stop.

options.text: Absorbing the children's momentum entirely
options.explanation: The momentum still falls to zero — just across a longer interval.

questions.stem: Which landing calls for the thickest crash mat?

options.text: A small child hopping off the final step
options.explanation: Low mass and low speed make this a gentle landing.

options.text: A slow sideways slip from standing height
options.explanation: A low-velocity fall carries little momentum.

options.text: A heavy adult dropping from a great height
options.explanation: Large mass and high speed mean the biggest momentum change, needing the longest contact time.

options.text: A light gymnast landing from a low beam
options.explanation: A light body and a small drop add up to a low-impact landing.

questions.stem: Thick mats are laid beneath bouldering walls because falls from the wall:

options.text: Carry enough momentum to need a long contact time on landing
options.explanation: A bouldering fall arrives with real speed, so a long, soft stop keeps the force safe.

options.text: Arrive more slowly than an ordinary stumble
options.explanation: Bouldering falls are quick — which is exactly why the mat is thick.

options.text: Gain no speed on the way down
options.explanation: Gravity accelerates the descent, which is part of why the stop is severe.

options.text: Need to be brought to rest as quickly as possible
options.explanation: Fast stops give big forces; the mat deliberately draws the stop out.

questions.stem: Why are gymnasium crash mats thick and soft?
questions.modelAnswer: So they can soak up the shock a landing body delivers and keep that body in touch with the mat for longer.

questions.stem: Name one place besides a gymnasium that cushions falls, and state how its surface helps.
questions.modelAnswer: Playgrounds use cushioned surfaces; the soft ground lengthens the child's contact time with the ground, so the impact force is smaller.

questions.stem: Explain why a soft crash mat makes a landing safer than a hard floor.
questions.modelAnswer: The mat stretches out the contact time, so the body's momentum changes over a longer interval; the rate of momentum change is smaller, so the peak landing force and the chance of injury both fall.

questions.stem: A 50 kg climber topples from a bouldering wall and lands at 4 m/s. A thick mat brings them to rest in 0.2 s; a bare floor would stop them in 0.02 s. Calculate the climber's momentum at landing and the average stopping force for each surface, then compare the two.
questions.modelAnswer: Momentum at landing is 50 × 4 = 200 kg·m/s. On the mat, F = 200 ÷ 0.2 = 1000 N; on the bare floor, F = 200 ÷ 0.02 = 10000 N. The mat's longer contact time makes its force ten times smaller.
